reason: This was the line I most expected to break, because the comma is the reading nobody quotes and the semicolon is the reading everybody quotes, so the burden was on the verifier. I downloaded all three texts and the verifier is right. Scan one, archive.org thoughtstrbywftr00pascuoft, title page THE HARVARD CLASSICS, BLAISE PASCAL, THOUGHTS, TRANSLATED BY W F TROTTER, P F COLLIER: fragment 347 at line 5529 reads Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature, but he is a thinking reed. Scan two, thoughtslettersm028185mbp, carrying Copyright, 1910 By P. F. COLLIER and SON on its verso, reads the same at line 5712. The comma is not an optical artifact: in the same paragraph both scans print semicolons correctly, scan one at him ; the universe knows nothing of this and at think well ; this is the principle of morality, scan two at him; the universe and atom; by thought. Project Gutenberg 18269, whose header names T. S. Eliot as author of introduction and whose title page reads A Dutton Paperback, E. P. DUTTON and CO., INC., prints the semicolon at line 5170, which is exactly where the proposal's wording came from. So the two printings of one translation genuinely differ and the note's account of it is accurate, including that the semicolon belongs to the later Dutton and Everyman printing. Brunschvicg: I also killed my own best objection here. The source line asserts Brunschvicg numbering, and I wondered whether that was an imported fact rather than the edition's claim, but the 1910 volume states it itself, at line 171 of scan two, The translation is from the text of Brunschvicg, and the Gutenberg Trotter adds that its notes are mainly based on those of M. Brunschvicg. Fragment 347 is where both print it. Locator right. Attribution right: Pascal's own note, not a reported line, no speaker owed, and it is not on the misattribution list. Quotation is a complete sentence ending in a full stop and the truncation does not misrepresent, since what follows develops the same thought. shipped.js: no exact match, no near match, not banned, but Pascal stands at two of three for the year with months 3 and 6, so this is his last line and the editor should know that before spending it. Scope: seventeenth century, published 1670, philosophy, publishable, nothing needing a warning. Source line 77 characters, leads with the name, no dash. Tag Philosophy is the form of the work. One imprecision worth fixing rather than refuting: the source line says Pensees while the edition whose comma it uses is titled Thoughts, so a reader who goes looking for Trotter alone will land on the Dutton semicolon text and think the card is wrong. Naming the printing in the parenthesis closes that gap and still fits, at 95 characters.
